tips.title: Square for area, cube for volume
tips.body: One length scale factor $k$ does three different things: lengths $\times k$, areas $\times k^2$, volumes $\times k^3$. Doubling every length quadruples the area and makes the volume **eight** times bigger.

tips.title: Units tell you which power you used
tips.body: A length answer is in cm, an area in cm², a volume in cm³. If a question asks for a volume and your working produced cm², you used $k^2$ where $k^3$ belonged. The units are a free check on the power.

tips.title: Route through the length ratio
tips.body: You cannot go from an area ratio to a volume ratio directly. **Square root** back to lengths, then **cube** forwards: areas $4 : 9$ give lengths $2 : 3$, so volumes $8 : 27$. Every backwards question is a root, every forwards one a power.

tips.title: Decide bigger or smaller first
tips.body: Before calculating, say whether the answer should be larger or smaller than what you started with. Then check it is. A scale factor used upside down always gives an answer that fails this test, and nothing else catches it.

steps.title: One length factor, three different effects
steps.body:
When a shape is **enlarged**, every length is multiplied by the **scale factor** $k$. What happens to its area and its volume follows from that, and it is not the same number.

- **Lengths** multiply by $k$
- **Areas** multiply by $k^2$
- **Volumes** multiply by $k^3$

Why? An area is a length times a length, so both get multiplied by $k$, giving $k \times k = k^2$. A volume is three lengths multiplied, giving $k^3$.

So doubling every length **quadruples** the area and makes the volume **eight** times bigger. That is why a scale model that looks twice as big has eight times the volume, and why a large animal is not simply a scaled-up small one.

The commonest error in the whole topic is multiplying an area by $k$ instead of $k^2$. If a question gives you an area or a volume, the scale factor you need is **never** just $k$.

steps.title: Going backwards
steps.body:
The harder questions give you the **areas** or the **volumes** and ask for a length. Then you must **undo** the power: square root for areas, cube root for volumes.

- Areas in the ratio $9 : 25$ mean lengths in the ratio $\sqrt{9} : \sqrt{25} = 3 : 5$.
- Volumes in the ratio $8 : 1$ mean lengths in the ratio $\sqrt[3]{8} : 1 = 2 : 1$.

This is the step that separates grades, because it is easy to reach for the wrong root or to forget the root altogether.

check.prompt: Two similar shapes have areas in the ratio 9 : 25. A side of the smaller is 6 cm. What is the matching side of the larger, in cm?
check.solution: Length ratio $= \sqrt{9} : \sqrt{25} = 3 : 5$, so the scale factor is $\dfrac{5}{3}$ and the side is $6 \times \dfrac{5}{3} = 10$ cm.

steps.title: Which way round is the scale factor?
steps.body:
A scale factor greater than 1 makes things **bigger**; less than 1 makes them **smaller**. Getting it upside down is the second commonest error here, and it always gives an answer that is wrong by a recognisable amount.

The habit that prevents it: **decide before you calculate whether the answer should be bigger or smaller than what you started with.** Then check your answer against that expectation.

- Going from the **smaller** shape to the **larger**, the scale factor is $\dfrac{\text{larger}}{\text{smaller}}$, and it is **greater than 1**.
- Going from **larger** to **smaller**, it is **less than 1**.

So if you enlarge something and your answer comes out smaller, you have used the reciprocal. One sentence of thought before the arithmetic catches it every time.

For **areas and volumes** the same logic applies to $k^2$ and $k^3$: a shape twice as long has four times the area, so going the other way its area is a **quarter**.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.** A cuboid measures 2 cm by 5 cm by 6 cm.

1. Work out its volume and its surface area.
2. It is enlarged by scale factor 4. Find the new volume and the new surface area.
3. Check your volume by working out the enlarged dimensions and multiplying.

**Part B.**

4. Two similar solids have volumes 27 cm³ and 216 cm³. Find the length scale factor.
5. The smaller solid is 4 cm wide. How wide is the larger?
6. The smaller has surface area 54 cm². What is the surface area of the larger?

**Part C.**

7. Explain why a scale model of a building is much lighter, relative to its size, than the real building.

For question 6, be careful: you already have the **length** scale factor from question 4, so use the right power.

visuals.alt: A blank table for the enlargement calculations, with a column for the power used

check.prompt: Two similar solids have volumes 27 cm³ and 216 cm³. What is the length scale factor from smaller to larger?
check.solution: Volume ratio $= 27 : 216 = 1 : 8$. Cube rooting gives the length ratio $1 : 2$, so the scale factor is **2**.

steps.title: Going deeper: ratios, and the two-step question
steps.body:
**Ratio notation.** The specification asks you to compare using **ratios**, and thinking in ratios avoids most errors. If lengths are in the ratio $a : b$, then

- areas are in the ratio $a^2 : b^2$;
- volumes are in the ratio $a^3 : b^3$.

So lengths $3 : 5$ give areas $9 : 25$ and volumes $27 : 125$. Written as a row it becomes hard to use the wrong power:

$$3 : 5 \quad\longrightarrow\quad 9 : 25 \quad\longrightarrow\quad 27 : 125$$

**The two-step question.** The hardest version gives you one kind of ratio and asks for another, so you have to pass **through the length ratio**.

> Two similar solids have surface areas in the ratio $4 : 9$. What is the ratio of their volumes?

You cannot go from areas to volumes directly. Square root the area ratio to get lengths $2 : 3$, then cube that to get volumes $8 : 27$.

**Always route through the length ratio.** Areas to lengths to volumes. Trying to jump gives $4^1.5$-style reasoning that is easy to get wrong and impossible to check.

**Units are a free check.** A length answer should be in cm, an area in cm², a volume in cm³. If a question asks for a volume and your working produced cm², you have used $k^2$ where $k^3$ belonged.

**One subtlety.** All of this needs the shapes to be **similar** — the same shape, different size. Two cuboids with the same volume but different proportions are not similar, and none of these rules apply to them. A question that says *mathematically similar* is telling you the rules are available; one that does not may be testing whether you noticed.

check.prompt: Two similar solids have surface areas in the ratio 4 : 9. What is the ratio of their volumes?
check.solution: Route through the **lengths**: $\sqrt{4} : \sqrt{9} = 2 : 3$, then cube to get $8 : 27$. Going straight from areas to volumes is not possible.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- With a length scale factor $k$: **lengths** $\times k$, **areas** $\times k^2$, **volumes** $\times k^3$.
- Doubling every length **quadruples** the area and makes the volume **8 times** bigger.
- Going **backwards** from an area, take the **square root**; from a volume, the **cube root**.
- In ratio form: lengths $a : b$ give areas $a^2 : b^2$ and volumes $a^3 : b^3$.
- To get from an **area ratio to a volume ratio**, route through the **length ratio**. You cannot jump.
- Decide before calculating whether the answer should be **bigger or smaller**, then check it is.
- A scale factor **greater than 1** enlarges; **less than 1** reduces.
- Areas and volumes scale differently, so the **ratio between them changes with size**. That is why small animals lose heat faster and model bridges are relatively stronger.
- **Units check the power**: cm for a length, cm² for an area, cm³ for a volume.
- All of it requires the shapes to be **mathematically similar**.
- The commonest error is multiplying an **area by $k$** instead of $k^2$.

questions.prompt: A shape has area 20 cm². It is enlarged so its lengths are 2.5 times bigger. What is the new area, in cm²?
Two mathematically similar solids have volumes 27 cm³ and 216 cm³. The smaller has surface area 54 cm² and is 4 cm wide. Find the width and the surface area of the larger solid.
questions.solution: Start from the volumes, which are in the ratio twenty seven to two hundred and sixteen. Dividing both by twenty seven gives one to eight. Because volume scales as the cube of the length scale factor, take the cube root of each part, which gives a length ratio of one to two, so the length scale factor from the smaller solid to the larger is two. The width of the larger solid is therefore four times two, which is eight centimetres. For the surface area, use the square of the length scale factor rather than the cube, because area scales as k squared. Two squared is four, so the surface area of the larger solid is fifty four times four, which is two hundred and sixteen square centimetres. As a check, the answers are both larger than the values for the smaller solid, as they should be for an enlargement.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The length scale factor.** Volumes $27 : 216 = 1 : 8$. Volume uses $k^3$, so cube root:

$$k = \sqrt[3]{8} = 2$$

**The width.** Lengths use $k$:

$$4 \times 2 = \mathbf{8} \text{ cm}$$

**The surface area.** Areas use $k^2 = 4$, **not** $k^3$:

$$54 \times 4 = \mathbf{216} \text{ cm}^2$$

**Check.** Both answers are larger than the originals, as an enlargement requires. And the units are right: cm for a width, cm² for an area.

The mark most often lost here is using $k^3$ for the surface area because the question began with volumes.

questions.prompt: Explain why a scale model of a bridge, built to one tenth of the real size, is far stronger relative to its own weight than the real bridge.
questions.solution: The strength of a supporting beam depends on its cross sectional area, and area scales as the square of the length scale factor. With a scale factor of one tenth, the cross sectional area of the model is one hundredth of the real one. The weight of the bridge, however, depends on its volume, and volume scales as the cube of the length scale factor, so the model weighs one thousandth of the real bridge. Comparing the two, the model has one hundredth of the strength but only one thousandth of the weight, so it has ten times as much strength for each unit of weight that it has to carry. This is why a model can be built from materials that would collapse at full size, and it is a direct consequence of area and volume scaling by different powers.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Strength follows area.** A beam's strength depends on its **cross-sectional area**, which scales as $k^2$. At one tenth size:

$$\left(\tfrac{1}{10}\right)^2 = \tfrac{1}{100}$$

**Weight follows volume.** Weight depends on **volume**, which scales as $k^3$:

$$\left(\tfrac{1}{10}\right)^3 = \tfrac{1}{1000}$$

**The comparison.** The model has $\tfrac{1}{100}$ of the strength but only $\tfrac{1}{1000}$ of the weight — so **ten times** as much strength for each unit of weight it must carry.

That is why a model can be built from materials that would collapse at full size, and it follows directly from **area and volume scaling by different powers**.

examTechnique.body:
Identify what you are given and what is wanted: a length, an area or a volume. That decides the power before any arithmetic.

Going forwards, multiply by $k$, $k^2$ or $k^3$. Going backwards, take the square root from an area or the cube root from a volume.

If a question gives one kind of ratio and asks for another, go **through the length ratio**. Never jump from areas to volumes.

Write the ratio chain down — lengths, areas, volumes — so the power you need is visible rather than remembered.

Decide whether the answer should be bigger or smaller before calculating, then check it against that.

Use the units as a final check: cm, cm² and cm³ each correspond to a different power.

And confirm the shapes are described as **mathematically similar** before applying any of it.
examinerErrors: Multiplying an area by k instead of k².
Multiplying a volume by k² instead of k³.
Taking a square root of a volume ratio, where a cube root belongs.
Going straight from an area ratio to a volume ratio without passing through the lengths.
Using the scale factor upside down, so an enlargement comes out smaller.
Giving a volume answer in cm².
Applying the rules to shapes that are not similar.
Working out all the new dimensions the long way when one multiplication would do.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer decides the power before touching the numbers, because it has identified whether it is holding a length, an area or a volume. Faced with a ratio of areas and a question about volumes, it writes the three-part chain and moves through the lengths rather than guessing an exponent. It sanity-checks direction and units without being asked, and when the question turns to a real situation it explains the effect in terms of area and volume scaling by **different powers**, which is the sentence the mark scheme is looking for.
